opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is recognizing that the web was built for humans, and search was built around human limitations. A human types a few keywords, looks at ten blue links, clicks on one or two, and does the synthesis in their own head. The whole system, including ranking, the interface, and the business model, is optimized for that. It's optimized for getting a click.

Agents are a fundamentally different customer. An agent doesn't get tired. It can read hundreds of pages, issue many queries in parallel, and it doesn't care about the visual layout. What it needs is the right tokens in its context window. So the question changes from "which ten links should I show?" to "what is the most relevant, information-dense set of content I can put in front of this model so it can reason well and complete the task?"

That has a few implications. First, the query looks different. Agents can express much richer intent, something closer to a full paragraph describing what they're trying to accomplish, rather than three keywords. Search should take advantage of that instead of collapsing it.

Second, the output looks different. You want to return compressed, relevant excerpts with provenance, not just URLs, because the agent's context is precious and every irrelevant token degrades reasoning.

Third, you have to think about the compute tradeoff explicitly. For some tasks you want a fast, cheap lookup. For others, it's worth spending minutes and a lot of compute to do deep research across the web and get something verifiably right. A search system for agents should expose that dial instead of pretending every query deserves the same budget.

And finally, I think verifiability and attribution matter more, not less. When an agent is taking actions on someone's behalf, you need to know where a fact came from and how confident you should be in it. So I'd say you build it from first principles for the machine as the reader, while keeping the open web healthy, so the people creating content still have reasons to keep creating it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human and agent search needs but does not argue that search should rely on agent feedback rather than human feedback.

r002.rationale: It recommends returning compressed excerpts, but does not identify models’ ability to compress information as a capability to improve search.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that search for agents is a fundamentally different product from search for humans, even though it looks superficially similar. Search for humans was built around ten blue links and a human sitting there deciding what to click on. The whole system was optimized for a person with limited attention, who wants something fast, scannable, and ranked so the right answer is near the top.

Agents don't have that constraint. An agent can read a hundred documents in the time it takes a person to read one. So the question isn't "what are the ten best links," it's "what is the complete set of information this model needs to answer the question well, and how do I get that into its context cleanly." That shifts the design center from ranking toward retrieval, coverage, and structure.

A few things follow from that. One is that the interface should be built around the model's needs rather than the human's. Models want the actual content, not snippets. They want it parsed, deduplicated, with the boilerplate stripped out, so the tokens they consume are high signal. They want to be able to issue many queries in parallel, refine, go deeper, and have the system be cheap and fast enough that doing that is normal rather than a luxury.

The second is that you have to think about freshness and the long tail really seriously. A lot of what agents are doing is not "what's the capital of France," it's finding the one obscure documentation page or the one GitHub issue or the one recent announcement that unlocks the task. So the index has to be broad and it has to be live, and the system has to be honest about when it doesn't know rather than confidently returning something stale.

Third, I think the model and the search system should be co-designed. The model is the consumer, and you can train it to use the tool well, and you can shape the tool around how the model actually behaves. That's a very different loop from the old world, where the search engine had to guess at human intent from two or three words.

And then the last thing is trust. If an agent is going to act on what it retrieves, provenance matters a lot more than it did when a person was in the loop. You want the sources attached, you want the model to know where things came from, and you want the system designed so that it's hard to poison. The incentives around search get even more adversarial when the consumer is a machine that will act on what it reads.

So in short: build it as infrastructure for models, not as a page for people. Optimize for completeness and quality of what ends up in context, make it fast and cheap enough to call constantly, keep it fresh, and make provenance a first-class part of the result.

r001.rationale: The response says the model and search system should be co-designed and that models can be trained to use the tool, but it does not argue that search should rely on agent feedback instead of human feedback.

r002.rationale: It says agents can read many documents quickly and describes cleaning and structuring retrieved content, but it does not identify models’ ability to compress information as a way to improve search.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what the agent is trying to accomplish. With human search, you return a set of links, and the person does a lot of the work: reading, comparing sources, deciding whether they have enough information. For an agent, search needs to make that work possible programmatically.

That means returning useful evidence with enough context to interpret it—where it came from, how fresh it is, and what it actually supports. The agent should be able to ask a broad question, learn something, and then narrow its search. It should also be able to recognize when the evidence is incomplete or conflicting.

And I’d measure the system by whether it helps the agent complete the task correctly. Did it find the information that mattered? Did it preserve the qualifications? Could it do that within the time and cost available? That’s the starting point I’d use for building search for agents.

r001.rationale: The response describes search supporting agents’ task completion and iterative narrowing, but does not argue that search should rely on agent feedback rather than human feedback.

r002.rationale: The response discusses returning contextual evidence, but does not identify models’ ability to compress information as a way to improve search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the fact that an agent uses search differently from a person. A person types a few words, looks at a page of links, and decides what to open. An agent might be in the middle of a task, discover that it’s missing some information, and need to go find it before continuing.

So I’d build around that workflow. Let the agent express what it needs in detail, return relevant information with clear sources, and make it easy to ask a follow-up question. Sometimes the right result is a short fact. Sometimes it’s a document or several sources that disagree. You want to preserve that distinction so the agent can reason about what it found.

And the measure of quality should be whether search helped the agent complete the task correctly. Did it find the evidence it needed? Was that evidence current? How much time and how many calls did it take? Those are the things I’d optimize for.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes agent search from a person’s search and evaluates whether it helps complete tasks, but it does not say search should rely on agent feedback rather than human feedback.

r002.rationale: The response discusses returning concise facts or documents, but does not identify models’ ability to compress information as a capability for improving search.
